title: Clause 14
text:
The supplier was six weeks late. The client wanted to cancel and claim damages. Both sides believed the contract was on their side.

It came down to clause 14, four lines long, written two years earlier by somebody who had since left the company.

The clause said delivery delays caused by "circumstances beyond reasonable control" would not be treated as a breach of contract. The supplier argued this was force majeure: the factory in Turkey had closed for three weeks after a flood.

The client's legal counsel read it differently. The flood was real, but the supplier had known about the closure for eleven days before telling anyone. The contract also required written notice within 48 hours of any delay.

That second point decided it. The delay might have been excusable; the silence was not.

They settled out of court. The supplier gave a 20% credit against the next order and both sides amended the contract to define notice more clearly.

The lawyer's comment afterwards was worth more than her invoice. Most disputes, she said, are not about what went wrong. They are about who said nothing when it did.

options: The delay was only two weeks
The supplier failed to give written notice in time

questions.q: What was the lawyer's main point?
options: Disputes often come from silence, not the original problem

title: The NDA that arrived too late
text:
A small software company met a potential partner in March. Over two friendly meetings they explained how their pricing model worked, including the part nobody else in the market had copied.

The non-disclosure agreement was signed in May.

By September the partner had launched a competing product using a very similar model. The software company asked its legal counsel whether it could sue.

The answer was uncomfortable. The NDA was properly drafted and binding, but it only covered information shared after the signature date. Everything explained in March sat outside it.

There was a second problem. The pricing model was a business idea, not intellectual property. It wasn't a patent, a trademark or copyright material. Ideas themselves are rarely protected; the specific expression of them sometimes is.

The company changed one habit after that. Nothing commercially sensitive is discussed until an NDA is signed, even in a friendly first meeting, and the agreement now includes information shared before the signature date.

It cost them a market advantage to learn a rule that fits in one sentence: sign first, talk second.

questions.q: Why couldn't the NDA help them?
options: It only covered information shared after signing

questions.q: Why was the pricing model not protected?
options: Ideas alone are rarely intellectual property

questions.q: What did the company change afterwards?
options: No sensitive talk before an NDA is signed
They moved to a different market

questions.q: What does "binding" mean in the text?
options: Legally forcing both sides to comply
